title: Tao Te Ching
subtitle: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
author: Laozi
description: The Tao Te Ching (Daodejing), the foundational classic of philosophical Taoism attributed to Laozi, the semi-legendary 'Old Master' said to have been a contemporary of Confucius, though the text probably took shape between the fifth and third centuries BCE. In eighty-one brief chapters of terse, paradoxical verse, it describes the Tao, the nameless Way that precedes heaven and earth, and its power or virtue (Te) as expressed in the sage. Recurring teachings include wu wei (effortless, non-coercive action), the strength of softness and water, emptiness as the source of usefulness, return to the uncarved block of simplicity, the relativity of opposites, the dangers of desire, cleverness and war, and government that rules by not interfering. One of the most translated books in the world, it underlies Taoist religion, Chinese medicine, internal alchemy and martial arts, influenced Chan and Zen Buddhism, and is read worldwide as a manual of contemplative and ethical wisdom.

title: Gleanings from the Writings of Baha'u'llah
author: Baha'u'llah
description: A core anthology of the writings of Baha'u'llah (1817-1892), founder of the Baha'i Faith, selected and translated into English by Shoghi Effendi and first published in 1935. Drawn from tablets and books revealed over four decades of exile in Baghdad, Adrianople and Akka, its 166 passages range across the nature of God as unknowable essence, the Manifestations of God as mirrors of the divine attributes, progressive revelation and the oneness of religion, the soul and its journey after death, the station of Baha'u'llah as the promised one of all ages, and the coming unity of humankind under just and peaceful world order. Ethical counsels on detachment, justice, trustworthiness and service sit alongside mystical meditations and prophetic summons to the kings and peoples of the world. Long regarded by Baha'is as the most representative single volume of their scripture, it is the standard entry point for readers wanting the theology, cosmology and social vision of the faith in its founder's own words.

title: Selections from the Writings of the Bab
author: The Bab
description: A compilation of the writings of the Bab (Siyyid Ali-Muhammad Shirazi, 1819-1850), the Persian prophet whose 1844 declaration began the Babi movement and who is regarded by Baha'is as the herald and forerunner of Baha'u'llah. Prepared by the Research Department of the Universal House of Justice and translated by Habib Taherzadeh (1976), it presents extracts from his major works, including the Qayyumu'l-Asma (commentary on the Surah of Joseph), the Persian Bayan, the Seven Proofs, the Book of Names and his addresses and prayers. Themes include the cyclical renewal of divine revelation, the expected advent of 'Him Whom God shall make manifest', the spiritual meaning of resurrection, judgement and paradise, the unity of the Prophets, and intense devotional praise of God. The Bab's ornate, symbol-laden style draws on Shi'i esoteric and Shaykhi thought, making this volume valuable both as Baha'i scripture and as a primary source for nineteenth-century Persian messianism and Islamic mysticism.

title: The Hidden Words
author: Baha'u'llah
description: A short classic of Baha'i devotional literature, revealed by Baha'u'llah around 1857-58 while walking along the banks of the Tigris during his exile in Baghdad, and translated by Shoghi Effendi. It consists of seventy-one brief Arabic and eighty-two Persian aphorisms addressed by God to the human soul ('O Son of Spirit', 'O Son of Being'). Baha'u'llah presented it as the inner essence of what was revealed to the earlier Prophets, clothed in brevity. The verses teach love of God as the purpose of creation, detachment from the world, purity of heart, justice, humility, the transience of material life and the soul's return to its Source. Its poetic concision, comparable to Sufi wisdom sayings and the Psalms, has made it one of the most widely read and memorised Baha'i texts and an accessible doorway into the mystical ethics of the faith.

title: The Kitab-i-Iqan
author: Baha'u'llah
description: The Kitab-i-Iqan (Book of Certitude), revealed by Baha'u'llah in Persian in 1861-62 in Baghdad in reply to questions from an uncle of the Bab, and translated by Shoghi Effendi. It is the principal doctrinal work of the Baha'i Faith. In two parts, it explains why each new Messenger of God has been rejected by the religious leaders of his day and interprets the apocalyptic symbols of earlier scripture (the darkening of the sun and moon, the falling of stars, the cloud, the resurrection and the Day of Judgement) as spiritual rather than literal events. It sets out the doctrine of progressive revelation, the station of the Manifestations of God, the meaning of the 'Seal of the Prophets', and the qualities of the true seeker, whose path of purification is described in a celebrated passage. Drawing heavily on the Qur'an, Bible and hadith, it is essential reading for Baha'i theology, comparative eschatology and the hermeneutics of sacred symbolism.

After a prelude on the human being as a diagram of everything, Part One sets out the problem of the primordial human: why the universe was imagined in human shape, four ways of reading 'in our image', and cosmogony through emanation, descent and counterpart. Later parts examine Adam Kadmon in Sefer Yetzirah, the Zohar and Lurianic Kabbalah, and the Anthropos in Nag Hammadi texts, before letting the two traditions argue over creation, the fall and restoration. It is useful as a thematic bridge between the library's Kabbalah and Gnostic holdings.

title: Raja Yoga
author: Swami Vivekananda
description: Swami Vivekananda's Raja Yoga (1896), the landmark book that introduced classical yoga to Western readers. Based on lectures given in New York in 1895-96, the first part explains the practice and philosophy of the 'royal path' of meditation in plain modern language: the need for concentration, the first steps of posture and breathing, the doctrine of prana and the psychic prana, control of the mind, pratyahara and dharana, dhyana and samadhi, and the awakening of kundalini along the sushumna. The second part is Vivekananda's own translation of and commentary on the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, organised in the four traditional chapters on concentration, practice, powers and independence (kaivalya). Presenting yoga as an experimental science of mind grounded in Vedanta and Samkhya, the book shaped the reception of yoga, meditation and Hindu spirituality throughout the twentieth century and remains a standard introduction.

title: The Diamond Sutra
author: Unknown
description: The Diamond Sutra (Vajracchedika Prajnaparamita Sutra), here in the Project Gutenberg edition titled The Diamond Sutra (Chin-Kang-Ching) or Prajna-Paramita, an early twentieth-century English translation from the Chinese with preface and introduction. One of the most revered texts of Mahayana Buddhism, it records a dialogue at Shravasti between the Buddha and his disciple Subhuti on the perfection of wisdom. The Buddha teaches that a bodhisattva must vow to liberate all beings while holding no notion of self, being, living entity or person; that all phenomena and even the Buddha's teaching are empty of fixed nature, like 'a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow'; and that merit from understanding even four lines of the sutra surpasses immeasurable gifts. Central to Chan and Zen (it famously enlightened Huineng), it is also the text of the oldest dated printed book, the Dunhuang copy of 868 CE.

It is a primary source for English Reformation religion and the language of English scripture.

title: The Wisdom of Solomon
author: Unknown
description: The Wisdom of Solomon, a book of the Apocrypha (deuterocanonical in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles), here in an early English translation with chapter divisions; the text is affected by OCR errors. Written in Greek in Alexandria probably in the first century BCE by a Hellenistic Jew writing in the persona of King Solomon, it addresses the rulers of the earth. Chapters 1-5 contrast the fate of the righteous and the ungodly and affirm the immortality of the soul. Chapters 6-9 praise personified Wisdom (Sophia), 'a breath of the power of God, and a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty', in language that influenced the Christian Logos doctrine and later Gnostic and Kabbalistic ideas of divine Wisdom. Chapters 10-19 review sacred history, especially the Exodus, as Wisdom's saving work, with a critique of idolatry. It is a key bridge text between Jewish scripture and Greek philosophy.

title: The Vision of God
author: Nicholas of Cusa (Salter trans)
description: The Vision of God (De visione Dei) by Nicholas of Cusa (1401-1464), translated by Emma Gurney Salter with an introduction by Evelyn Underhill (1928). Written in 1453 for the Benedictine monks of Tegernsee, the treatise accompanied a painted 'all-seeing' icon whose eyes seem to follow every viewer. Cusanus asks the monks to experience how the gaze rests on each of them at once, and from this exercise develops a meditation on God's seeing as God's being and creating. In twenty-five chapters addressed in prayer to God, he explores the coincidence of opposites as the 'wall of paradise' beyond which God dwells, infinity, love, the Trinity, and Jesus as the consummation in whom the divine and human are united. A jewel of late medieval mystical theology, it joins Dionysian apophaticism with a new perspectival vision and is a key bridge to Renaissance thought.

title: On Learned Ignorance
author: Nicholas of Cusa (Hopkins trans)
description: On Learned Ignorance (De docta ignorantia) by Nicholas of Cusa, in the English translation by Jasper Hopkins (Arthur J. Banning Press, 1981; 2nd ed. 1985), with notes. Completed in 1440, it is Cusanus's founding philosophical work. Book One treats the Absolute Maximum, God, as beyond all comparison and proportion, knowable only through a 'learned ignorance' that recognises the limits of reason; using mathematical symbols (the infinite line, triangle, circle and sphere), Cusanus shows how opposites coincide in the infinite. Book Two treats the universe as the 'contracted maximum', with famous anticipations of modern cosmology: the world has no fixed centre or circumference and the earth is not at rest. Book Three treats Jesus Christ as the maximum both absolute and contracted, uniting God and creation. A turning point between medieval mysticism and Renaissance philosophy, it influenced Bruno, Kepler and later speculative thought.

title: Timaeus
author: Plato (Jowett trans)
description: Timaeus by Plato, in the classic translation of Benjamin Jowett (Oxford, first edition 1871), with his introduction and analysis. Written around 360 BCE, the dialogue opens with Critias's tale of Atlantis and ancient Athens before Timaeus of Locri delivers a 'likely story' of cosmic creation. A good divine craftsman, the Demiurge, looking to eternal Forms, shapes the visible cosmos as a living being with a World Soul, made in the image of the eternal, with time as 'a moving image of eternity'. Timaeus describes the planetary circles, the receptacle or chora, the construction of the four elements from triangles corresponding to the regular solids, and the formation of the human body, soul, senses and diseases. The most influential Platonic dialogue in antiquity and the Middle Ages, it underlies Neoplatonism, Hermeticism, sacred geometry, Kepler's cosmology and the Atlantis legend.

title: Harmonices Mundi (Latin, 1619)
author: Johannes Kepler
description: Harmonices Mundi Libri V (The Harmony of the World), Johannes Kepler's Latin masterwork published at Linz in 1619. Kepler regarded it as his greatest achievement, and in it he seeks the divine harmonic order underlying geometry, music, astrology and the cosmos. Book I treats regular polygons and their constructibility; Book II the congruence of polygons and polyhedra, including the first systematic treatment of tilings and the discovery of two new star polyhedra; Book III the mathematical basis of musical consonance; Book IV the harmonic configurations of the heavens in astrology and the nature of the soul; and Book V the 'music of the spheres', where he relates the planets' extreme angular velocities to musical intervals and announces his third law of planetary motion (the squares of periods are proportional to the cubes of mean distances). It is the culmination of the Pythagorean-Platonic quest for cosmic harmony and a founding document of modern astronomy.

title: Mysterium Cosmographicum (Latin, 1596)
author: Johannes Kepler
description: Mysterium Cosmographicum (The Cosmographic Mystery), Johannes Kepler's first major work, published in Latin at Tübingen in 1596. A passionate defence of the Copernican heliocentric system, it proposes that the number, distances and order of the six then-known planets are explained by nesting the five Platonic solids (cube, tetrahedron, dodecahedron, icosahedron and octahedron) between the planetary spheres, a design Kepler believed revealed the geometric plan by which God created the universe. He also suggests that a force emanating from the Sun moves the planets, the seed of physical astronomy, and compares his model with observational data. The theory was later superseded, but the book launched Kepler's career, brought him to the attention of Tycho Brahe and Galileo, and shows the fusion of Pythagorean sacred geometry, theology and empirical science at the birth of modern astronomy.

title: Tetrabiblos
author: Ptolemy (Ashmand trans)
description: Tetrabiblos (Quadripartitum, 'Four Books') by Claudius Ptolemy of Alexandria (second century CE), in the English translation by J. M. Ashmand (1822), with an appendix of related material from the Almagest on the aspects of the fixed stars. The most authoritative astrological text of the ancient and medieval world, it presents astrology as a natural science of celestial influence complementary to Ptolemy's astronomy. Book I defends astrology's possibility and sets out the powers of the planets, the signs, triplicities, houses, terms and aspects. Book II covers mundane astrology: the influence of the heavens on countries and peoples, eclipses and weather. Books III and IV treat the nativity: parents, siblings, sex, length of life, bodily form, temperament and disease, the quality of the soul, wealth, honour, marriage, children, travel and manner of death. It shaped Arabic, medieval and Renaissance astrology and remains a foundation of traditional practice.

title: Divina Proportione (Italian, 1509)
author: Luca Pacioli
description: Divina Proportione (On the Divine Proportion) by the Franciscan mathematician Luca Pacioli, printed in Italian in Venice in 1509 with sixty illustrations of polyhedra drawn by his friend Leonardo da Vinci. The first part, the Compendium de divina proportione, studies the 'divine proportion' (the golden ratio, or extreme and mean ratio), listing its thirteen 'effects' and its theological significance as a proportion that, like God, is unique and cannot be expressed rationally, and applies it to the regular and semi-regular solids. Further sections treat architecture and the proportions of the human body after Vitruvius, the design of Roman capital letters, and an Italian translation of Piero della Francesca's work on the regular solids. A landmark of Renaissance mathematics and art theory, it gave the golden ratio its sacred name and underpins later sacred-geometry traditions.

author: Julius Firmicus Maternus
description: Matheseos Libri VIII, Volume 1, by Julius Firmicus Maternus, in the Latin critical edition by Wilhelm Kroll and Franz Skutsch (Leipzig: Teubner, 1897), containing Books I-IV and the preface to Book V. Written around 334-337 CE by a Sicilian rhetorician who later converted to Christianity, the Mathesis is the longest and most complete surviving Latin manual of astrology. Book I defends astrology against its critics and argues that the stars signify rather than compel human fate. Following books explain the signs, planets, houses, aspects, decans and lots, and give hundreds of interpretations of planetary positions in the nativity, drawing on Hellenistic sources attributed to Nechepso, Petosiris, Hermes and Abraham. It preserves the famous 'Thema Mundi', the horoscope of the world's birth. It is a key source for Hellenistic astrology and Hermetic cosmology in the Latin West.

title: Aurora, the Day-Spring
author: Jakob Bohme (Sparrow trans)
description: Aurora (Morgenröte im Aufgang, 'The Day-Spring or Morning Redness in the Rising of the Sun') by Jakob Böhme (1575-1624), the Lutheran shoemaker-mystic of Görlitz, in the seventeenth-century English translation by John Sparrow (1656), edited in modern reprints by C. J. Barker and D. S. Hehner. Written in 1612 after a visionary illumination, it is Böhme's first book, and its circulation led to his being forbidden to write by the local pastor. It describes 'the root or mother of philosophy, astrology and theology' through an account of God's nature as dynamic interplay of qualities or 'source-spirits', the Trinity, the creation and fall of the angels and Lucifer, and the origin of good and evil, the heavens, the stars and the elements. Dense and visionary, it founded the theosophical tradition that influenced German Idealism, Romanticism, William Law, Blake and later Christian esotericism.

title: Signatura Rerum, the Signature of All Things
author: Jakob Bohme
description: Signatura Rerum: The Signature of All Things by Jakob Böhme (1622), in the English translation by John Ellistone (1651), often reprinted in Everyman's Library. In it the Silesian mystic shows how the inner spiritual essence of every created thing is expressed in its outward form, colour, smell and sound, its 'signature', so that nature is a language revealing God. Böhme describes the seven qualities or forms of eternal nature by which the divine will manifests out of the Ungrund, the generation of the 'eternal word', the contest of wrath and love, and the redemption of fallen creation through Christ. He uses the language of alchemy (salt, sulphur and mercury, the philosophers' stone, the planetary metals) as a symbolic key to the soul's rebirth. It is foundational for Christian theosophy, Paracelsian correspondence theory and the doctrine of signatures in esoteric medicine.

title: On the Divine Names and The Mystical Theology
author: Pseudo-Dionysius (Rolt trans)
description: Dionysius the Areopagite on the Divine Names and the Mystical Theology, translated with an introduction by C. E. Rolt (SPCK, 1920). The author, writing around 500 CE under the name of St Paul's Athenian convert, fused Christian theology with the Neoplatonism of Proclus, and his works became authoritative in both Eastern and Western Christianity. The Divine Names examines the names given to God in scripture, such as Good, Light, Beauty, Love, Being, Life, Wisdom, Power, Peace and One, interpreting them as the processions of the divine into creation while affirming that God transcends all names. The brief Mystical Theology teaches the way of negation: ascending beyond all affirmations and denials into the 'divine darkness' of unknowing where God is met beyond knowledge. Rolt's long introduction relates the works to Neoplatonism and later mysticism. These texts founded Christian apophatic theology and shaped Eriugena, Aquinas, Eckhart, the Cloud of Unknowing and Cusanus.

description: Gregory of Nyssa: Dogmatic Treatises, etc., Volume V of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, edited by Philip Schaff and Henry Wace (1893), translated by William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson. Gregory's teaching on God's infinity, the soul's endless ascent (epektasis), and universal restoration shaped Christian mysticism from Dionysius to the Orthodox tradition.

title: Meister Eckhart, Vol. 1
author: Meister Eckhart (Evans trans)
description: Meister Eckhart, Volume 1, translated by C. de B. Evans (London: John M. Watkins, 1924) from the edition of Franz Pfeiffer (Leipzig, 1857), 'with some omissions and additions'. Eckhart von Hochheim (c. 1260-1328), Dominican friar, Paris master and preacher, is the greatest of the German mystics, and some of his propositions were condemned in 1329. This volume gathers his German sermons and collations, presenting his central teachings: the birth of the Word in the ground of the soul, the 'spark' or uncreated something in the soul, detachment (Abgeschiedenheit) and letting-be (Gelassenheit), the distinction between God and the Godhead beyond God, the breakthrough into the silent desert of the divine essence, and living 'without a why'. The Evans translation was the main English Eckhart for decades and influenced Theosophical, Traditionalist and comparative interest in him alongside Vedanta and Zen.

title: The Cloud of Unknowing
author: Anonymous (Underhill ed)
description: The Cloud of Unknowing, the anonymous fourteenth-century English mystical treatise, edited from the British Museum manuscript with an introduction by Evelyn Underhill (1912). Written by an unknown contemplative priest, probably in the East Midlands, for a young disciple called to the solitary life, it teaches a method of contemplative prayer rooted in the apophatic tradition of Pseudo-Dionysius. God cannot be grasped by the intellect but may be reached by love: the contemplative places all created things, thoughts and even holy images beneath a 'cloud of forgetting' and directs a 'naked intent' of love, often focused in a single short word such as 'God' or 'love', into the 'cloud of unknowing' between the soul and God. Across seventy-five short chapters it gives practical advice on distractions, humility, discretion and signs of a true calling. A classic of English spirituality, it inspired modern centering prayer.

title: Revelations of Divine Love
author: Julian of Norwich (Warrack ed)
description: Revelations of Divine Love by Julian of Norwich (c. 1342-after 1416), edited by Grace Warrack from the British Museum Sloane manuscript (Methuen, 1901), the edition that made Julian widely known. An anchoress at St Julian's Church in Norwich, she received sixteen 'shewings' during a severe illness in May 1373 and spent twenty years reflecting on them, producing the earliest surviving book in English known to be written by a woman. The visions centre on Christ's Passion and reveal the overwhelming love of God. Themes include the hazelnut as an image of all creation held in being by love, the parable of the lord and the servant reinterpreting the Fall, sin as 'behovely', the motherhood of God and Christ, and the assurance that 'all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well'. Warrack supplies an introduction and glossary. It is one of the most beloved works of Christian mysticism.

title: Cherubinischer Wandersmann (German)
author: Angelus Silesius
description: Cherubinischer Wandersmann (The Cherubinic Wanderer) by Angelus Silesius (Johann Scheffler, 1624-1677), in the original German. A Silesian physician who converted to Catholicism and became a priest, Scheffler first published the work in 1657 as Geistreiche Sinn- und Schlussreime, enlarging it to six books in 1675. It contains over 1,600 rhymed epigrams, mostly in alexandrine couplets, distilling the mystical theology of Eckhart, Tauler, Ruysbroeck and Böhme into paradoxes such as 'Die Ros ist ohn warum' ('The rose is without why') and 'I know that without me God cannot live an instant'. Themes include the birth of God in the soul, divine nothingness, detachment, union and the interchange of God and creature. A classic of German Baroque literature and mystical poetry, it influenced Leibniz, Hegel, Schopenhauer and Heidegger and remains much quoted in comparative mysticism.

title: The Mirror of Simple Souls
author: Marguerite Porete (Kirchberger ed)
description: The Mirror of Simple Souls, attributed to Marguerite Porete, edited by Clare Kirchberger (London: Burns Oates and Washbourne, Orchard Books series, 1927) from the Middle English translation made from a French original. Porete, a beguine from Hainaut, was burned in Paris in 1310 after refusing to recant the book; her authorship was only identified in 1946, so this edition presents it as the work of an anonymous fourteenth-century mystic. Written as a dialogue among Love, Reason, the Soul and other allegorical figures, it describes seven stages by which the 'annihilated' or 'simple' soul passes beyond the guidance of Reason and the works of virtue into a state of union where it wills nothing but God's will and is at rest in divine love. Kirchberger's introduction discusses the manuscripts and the glosses of the English translator 'M.N.'. It is a key text of beguine mysticism and the 'Free Spirit' controversy.

title: The Spiritual Espousals
author: John of Ruysbroeck
description: The Spiritual Espousals (Die Gheestelike Brulocht) by Jan van Ruusbroec (John of Ruysbroeck, 1293-1381), the Flemish priest and contemplative of Groenendaal, here in an English translation of the 1940s-50s by Eric Colledge, made from the Ruusbroec-Genootschap critical edition (1932) and with introduction and bibliography. Ruusbroec's masterpiece, written in Middle Dutch around 1335, is structured around Christ's words 'See, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet him' (Matthew 25:6). Its three books describe three levels of life: the active life of virtue and moral striving, the interior or yearning life of devotion and union with God through grace, and the contemplative or 'God-seeing' life, in which the soul is united with God without intermediary in the dark, fruitful silence of the divine essence and the life of the Trinity. A classic of Low Countries mysticism, it influenced the Devotio Moderna, Tauler and later Catholic spirituality.

title: Theologia Germanica
author: Anonymous (Winkworth trans)
description: Theologia Germanica, the anonymous fourteenth-century German mystical treatise, in the English translation by Susanna Winkworth (London, 1854), made from the edition of Franz Pfeiffer, with prefaces including one by Charles Kingsley. Written by an unnamed priest of the Teutonic Order in Frankfurt (the 'Frankfurter'), probably in the later fourteenth century in the circle of the Friends of God, it was discovered and printed by Martin Luther in 1516 and 1518, who said that, after the Bible and Augustine, no book had taught him more about God, Christ and humanity. In fifty-odd short chapters it teaches that sin is self-will, the creature's claim to be something in itself, and that salvation lies in the death of selfhood and the union of the human will with the eternal Good. It describes the 'true light' and the false light, the life of Christ as the best life, obedience and poverty of spirit, and deification. It influenced Lutheran piety, Pietism, Johann Arndt and later Protestant mysticism, and was placed on the Catholic Index.

description: Select Revelations of S. Mechtild, Virgin, taken from the five books of her Spiritual Grace and translated from the Latin by 'a secular priest' (London: T. title: Heaven and its Wonders and Hell

description: Heaven and its Wonders and Hell, from Things Heard and Seen (De Caelo et ejus Mirabilibus et de Inferno, London, 1758) by Emanuel Swedenborg (1688-1772), the Swedish scientist and visionary, in English translation. Swedenborg's most widely read work, it describes the spiritual world he claimed to have visited over many years. In 603 numbered sections it explains that God is visible in heaven as the spiritual sun of divine love, that heaven has the form of one 'Grand Man', the correspondences between spiritual and natural things, the life, homes, work, language and marriages of angels, the world of spirits where people go after death, the human being's state after death, and the nature of hell, which people choose according to their ruling love; freedom depends on the equilibrium between heaven and hell. It influenced Blake, Emerson, Balzac, Spiritualism and the doctrine of correspondences across later esotericism.

title: The Song Celestial, or Bhagavad Gita
author: Edwin Arnold (trans)
description: The Song Celestial, or Bhagavad-Gita (from the Mahabharata), Sir Edwin Arnold's verse translation first published in 1885, being a discourse between Arjuna, Prince of India, and the Supreme Being under the form of Krishna. Arnold, author of The Light of Asia, rendered the 700-verse Sanskrit poem into flowing English blank verse and lyric metres. It was through this translation that the young Mohandas Gandhi first read the Gita in London. On the battlefield of Kurukshetra, Arjuna despairs at fighting his kinsmen, and Krishna teaches him in eighteen chapters on the immortal Self, duty (dharma), the yoga of selfless action, knowledge and devotion, the nature of Brahman and the three gunas, and reveals his universal cosmic form. The Gita is the most influential text of Hindu spirituality, central to Vedanta and to Theosophy, Transcendentalism and modern yoga.

title: The Secret of Recognition (Pratyabhijnahrdayam)
author: Kshemaraja (Leidecker trans)
description: The Secret of Recognition (Pratyabhijnahrdayam, 'The Heart of Recognition') by Kshemaraja, translated by Kurt F. Leidecker with the Sanskrit text and notes (Adyar Library, 1938). Kshemaraja (c. 975-1025 CE), the foremost disciple of Abhinavagupta, wrote this concise manual of twenty sutras with his own commentary to make the subtle Pratyabhijna ('Recognition') school of Kashmir Shaivism accessible to those without philosophical training. It teaches that supreme Consciousness (Chiti), free and self-luminous, is the cause of the universe; that it contracts itself into the limited individual and the world, and that liberation consists in recognising one's identity with Shiva. It explains the five acts of Shiva, the categories (tattvas), the expansion of the centre (madhya) and practices such as the unfolding of the heart. A key primer on non-dual Tantric Shaivism, it has become central to modern interest in Kashmir Shaivism.

description: The Upanishads, translated and commented on by Swami Paramananda (1884-1940) of the Ramakrishna Order, founder of the Vedanta Centre in Boston and Ananda Ashrama in California (Volume I, 1919). The Upanishads are the philosophical culmination of the Vedas and the source of Vedanta's teaching that Atman and Brahman are one. Paramananda's version is valued for its devotional clarity.

description: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, translated from the Chinese by Herbert A. Giles (London: Bernard Quaritch, 1889; revised 1926), the first complete English translation of the Zhuangzi. Zhuangzi (Chuang Tzu, c. 369-286 BCE) is, with Laozi, the founding figure of philosophical Taoism. The work's thirty-three chapters combine philosophy, parable and humour: the giant Peng bird, Cook Ding carving the ox, the useless tree, the frog in the well, the debate on the happiness of fish, Zhuangzi dreaming he was a butterfly, and his drumming and singing at his wife's death. Its teaching celebrates spontaneity, the relativity of all perspectives, the equality of things, the free and easy wandering of the sage, and acceptance of death and change in harmony with the Tao. Giles's introduction and notes present Zhuangzi as a critic of Confucian moralism. It is a primary text for Taoist mysticism and later Chan and Zen.

title: The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali
author: Charles Johnston (trans)
description: The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali: The Book of the Spiritual Man, an interpretation by Charles Johnston (1867-1931), the Irish Theosophist and Sanskritist (1912). The Yoga Sutras, compiled by Patanjali in the early centuries CE, are the foundational text of classical Raja Yoga: 196 aphorisms in four books defining yoga as the stilling of the fluctuations of consciousness (chitta vritti nirodha). Book I explains concentration and the states of samadhi; Book II the means of practice, the kleshas and the eightfold path of restraints, observances, posture, breath, withdrawal, concentration, meditation and absorption; Book III the powers (siddhis) arising from samyama; and Book IV liberation as the isolation (kaivalya) of pure seeing. Johnston's version offers translation with commentary interpreting the sutras in terms of the 'spiritual man' emerging from the 'psychic man', reflecting Theosophical and Christian mystical sympathies.

Traditionally attributed to Adi Shankara (eighth century CE), the great exponent of Advaita Vedanta, this poem of some 580 verses is cast as a dialogue between a teacher and a disciple seeking freedom from the cycle of birth and death. It teaches the qualifications of the seeker, discrimination between the real and the unreal, the five sheaths (koshas) that veil the Self, the three bodies and three states of consciousness, the superimposition (adhyasa) of the not-self on the Self, and the realisation that Atman is identical with Brahman, the attainment of jivanmukti or liberation in life. title: The Hymn of the Robe of Glory
author: G. R. S. Mead
description: The Hymn of the Robe of Glory by G. R. S. Mead (London: Theosophical Publishing Society, 1908), Volume V of his 'Echoes from the Gnosis' series. The hymn, also known as the Hymn of the Pearl, is a Syriac poem preserved in the apocryphal Acts of Thomas, probably composed in the Edessan milieu of the second or third century. It tells of a royal prince sent from the East by his parents, the King of Kings and the Queen of the East, down into Egypt to recover a pearl guarded by a serpent. He forgets his mission in the foreign land until a letter from home awakens him; he charms the serpent, takes the pearl and returns to put on his radiant robe of glory, which reflects his true self. Mead provides an introduction and a translation with commentary interpreting the hymn as an allegory of the soul's descent, forgetting, awakening and return. It is one of the most beautiful expressions of Gnostic soteriology.

title: The Odes and Psalms of Solomon
author: J. Rendel Harris (trans)
description: The Odes and Psalms of Solomon, published from the Syriac version by J. Rendel Harris (Cambridge University Press, 1909; second edition 1911), with introduction, translation and notes. Harris, the Quaker biblical scholar and manuscript hunter, discovered in 1909 a Syriac manuscript among his own papers containing the forty-two Odes of Solomon, previously known only from quotations in the Pistis Sophia, together with the eighteen Psalms of Solomon. The Psalms of Solomon are Jewish poems of the first century BCE lamenting Pompey's capture of Jerusalem and longing for the Davidic Messiah. The Odes, probably composed in Syria around the late first or early second century CE, are the earliest Christian hymnbook: ecstatic songs of union with the Lord, the living water, the crown of truth, the Word and the descent into Hades, with mystical and proto-Gnostic tones. Harris's discovery was a sensation and the Odes are central to the study of early Christian mysticism and liturgy.

title: The Gnostic John the Baptizer
author: G. R. S. Mead
description: The Gnostic John the Baptizer: Selections from the Mandaean John-Book by G. R. S. Mead (London: John M. Watkins, 1924). The Mandaeans of southern Iraq and Iran, the last surviving Gnostic community, revere John the Baptist as their great teacher and practise repeated baptism in flowing 'living water'. Mead translates, largely from Mark Lidzbarski's German edition of the Mandaean Book of John (Drashe d-Yahya), the passages concerning John: his miraculous birth, his teaching and baptisms in the Jordan, his dialogues with the 'Messiah' and the Jews, and his death and ascent to the world of light. Introductory chapters survey Mandaean origins, cosmology and the controversy over their relation to early Christianity and the Gospel of John, and the book closes with essays on John the Baptist in Christian and Josephan tradition. It is an accessible early English gateway to Mandaean literature.

title: Monas Hieroglyphica (Latin, 1591)
author: John Dee
description: Monas Hieroglyphica (The Hieroglyphic Monad) by John Dee (1527-1608/9), the Elizabethan mathematician, astrologer and magus, here in a Latin edition dated 1591 (the work was first printed at Antwerp in 1564 and dedicated to the Emperor Maximilian II). In twenty-four theorems Dee presents a single composite glyph, the Monad, combining the symbols of the Moon, Sun, the cross of the elements and the sign of Aries, and expounds it geometrically, arithmetically, astronomically, alchemically and Kabbalistically as a universal key unifying all knowledge and expressing the structure of creation. Dee claimed the Monad would revolutionise astronomy, alchemy, mathematics, languages and mechanics. Notoriously cryptic, it influenced the Rosicrucian manifestos (the Monad appears in the Chymical Wedding of Christian Rosenkreutz) and remains a central text of Renaissance Hermetic and alchemical symbolism.

title: Commentaries of Proclus on Euclid, Vol. 1
author: Proclus (Taylor trans)
description: The Philosophical and Mathematical Commentaries of Proclus on the First Book of Euclid's Elements, Volume 1, translated from the Greek by Thomas Taylor (London, 1788-89; reissued 1792), with a preliminary dissertation on the Platonic doctrine of ideas and other essays. Proclus (412-485 CE), head of the Neoplatonic school at Athens, wrote the most important surviving ancient commentary on Euclid, valuable both for the history of Greek mathematics (preserving the 'Eudemian summary' of early geometers from Thales to Euclid) and for its philosophy of mathematics. This first volume contains Proclus's two prologues, which present mathematical objects as intermediate between the sensible world and the divine Forms, explain how geometry awakens the soul's innate reasons and leads it toward theology, and discuss the Pythagorean view of number and figure, followed by commentary on Euclid's definitions. Taylor's notes connect it to Pythagorean and Platonic mysticism. It is a foundational text for the philosophy behind sacred geometry.

description: The Philosophical and Mathematical Commentaries of Proclus on the First Book of Euclid's Elements, Volume 2, translated by Thomas Taylor (London, 1788-89; reissued 1792), completing his English version with Proclus's detailed commentary on the postulates, axioms and propositions of Euclid's first book, up to the Pythagorean theorem and its converse. Taylor adds his own translations and notes, including material on Pythagorean and Platonic mathematics. Together with Volume 1, it shows how late antique Platonists treated mathematics as a ladder to the divine and is a key source for the Neoplatonic philosophy of geometry.

description: The Enneads, Volume 1, of Plotinus (c. 204-270 CE), in the translation by Stephen MacKenna (London: Medici Society, from 1917), the celebrated English rendering of the founder of Neoplatonism. MacKenna's lyrical translation, a lifelong labour, shaped the English reception of Neoplatonic mysticism.

title: The Theology of Plato and Elements of Theology
author: Proclus (Taylor trans)
description: The Theology of Plato, by Proclus (412-485 CE), translated by Thomas Taylor (London, 1816), bound or associated with his Elements of Theology. Proclus, head of the Platonic Academy at Athens, produced in the Platonic Theology the most systematic exposition of late Neoplatonic theology. In six books he extracts from Plato's dialogues a complete hierarchy of divine principles: the One, the henads or gods, and the intelligible, intellectual and supermundane orders, interpreting the Parmenides, Timaeus, Phaedrus and other dialogues as a revealed theology. The Elements of Theology sets out 211 propositions, in the manner of Euclid, deriving the structure of reality from the One through procession and return. Taylor's translation, the first in English, carried Neoplatonism into English Romanticism and later esoteric movements. It is a cornerstone of systematic Neoplatonic metaphysics.

description: The Life of Pythagoras, with his Symbols and Golden Verses, together with the Life of Hierocles and his Commentaries upon the Verses, translated from the French of André Dacier (first published in English in 1707, the version here attributed in the index to Dacier and Nicholas Rowe). Dacier's life of Pythagoras gathers ancient testimonies on the Samian sage's travels to Egypt and the East, his community at Croton, his teaching on number, harmony, the transmigration of souls, purification and silence, and the death of the master. The Golden Verses are the short Pythagorean poem of moral and spiritual precepts. The commentary of Hierocles of Alexandria, a fifth-century Neoplatonist, interprets them as a complete course of philosophical life, from civic virtue through purification to deification. It is an important early modern vehicle for the Pythagorean revival in English esotericism.

title: 3 Enoch, or The Hebrew Book of Enoch
author: Hugo Odeberg (ed)
description: 3 Enoch, or The Hebrew Book of Enoch, edited and translated for the first time with introduction, commentary and critical notes by Hugo Odeberg (Cambridge University Press, 1928), with the Hebrew text. Also known as Sefer Hekhalot, the book belongs to Merkavah and Hekhalot mysticism and was probably redacted between the fifth and ninth centuries CE. It presents Rabbi Ishmael's ascent through the heavenly palaces to the divine throne, where he meets Metatron, who reveals that he was once the patriarch Enoch, transformed into a fiery angelic being, enthroned as the 'lesser YHWH' and prince of the divine presence. Metatron describes the angelic hierarchies, the celestial court, the curtain (pargod) on which all history is written, the souls of the righteous and the wicked, and the cosmic secrets. Odeberg's edition is a landmark of Jewish mysticism scholarship and a key link between apocalyptic Enoch literature and Kabbalah.

title: Etz Chaim (The Tree of Life)
author: Chaim Vital (Sefaria Community trans)
description: Etz Chaim (The Tree of Life) by Rabbi Chaim Vital (1543-1620), here in the community English translation from Sefaria. Vital was the chief disciple of Isaac Luria (the Ari) in sixteenth-century Safed, and Etz Chaim is the principal systematic presentation of Lurianic Kabbalah. Organised into 'palaces' and 'gates', it begins with the hall of Adam Kadmon and the round and direct lights, and describes tzimtzum (God's self-contraction to make space for creation), the line of light (kav), Adam Kadmon and the lights emanating from his eyes, ears, nose and mouth, the shattering of the vessels (shevirat ha-kelim), the partzufim or divine 'faces' (Arikh Anpin, Abba, Imma, Zeir Anpin and Nukva), the worlds of Atzilut, Beriah, Yetzirah and Assiyah, and tikkun, the restoration of the world through human action. It is the foundation of all later Kabbalah and essential for the library's Adam Kadmon studies.

title: Pardes Rimonim (Orchard of Pomegranates)
author: Moses Cordovero (Sefaria Community trans)
description: Pardes Rimonim (Orchard of Pomegranates) by Rabbi Moses Cordovero (the Ramak, 1522-1570), the leading Kabbalist of Safed before Isaac Luria, here in the community English translation from Sefaria. Completed around 1548 and divided into thirty-two 'gates', it is the first comprehensive systematisation of Kabbalah, reconciling the diverse views in the Zohar and earlier Kabbalists. Cordovero discusses the Ein Sof and its relation to the sefirot, whether the sefirot are God's essence or vessels, their order, emanation and names, the divine names and their combinations, the channels connecting the sefirot, the worlds, the soul, the 'shells' (kelippot), and the mysteries of letters, vowels and prayer. Its rigorous, philosophical approach made it the classic textbook of pre-Lurianic Kabbalah.

title: Sepher Yetzirah
author: W. Wynn Westcott (trans)
description: Sepher Yetzirah (The Book of Formation and the Thirty-Two Paths of Wisdom), translated from the Hebrew with annotations by W. Wynn Westcott (first published 1887; later editions 1893 and 1911), the Freemason and co-founder of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. The Sefer Yetzirah, perhaps composed between the second and sixth centuries CE, is the oldest surviving text of Jewish esoteric cosmology. In a few terse chapters it describes how God created the world through the thirty-two paths of wisdom: the ten sefirot ('numbers' or 'spheres') and the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet, divided into three mothers (Aleph, Mem, Shin), seven doubles and twelve simples, corresponding to elements, planets, days, zodiac signs and parts of the body. Westcott adds notes and the Thirty-Two Paths of Wisdom attributed to it. His version shaped the Golden Dawn's attribution of Hebrew letters and Tarot to the Tree of Life.

title: The Kabbalah Unveiled
author: S. L. MacGregor Mathers (trans)
description: The Kabbalah Unveiled (Kabbala Denudata), translated into English by S. L. MacGregor Mathers (London, 1887) from the Latin of Christian Knorr von Rosenroth's Kabbala Denudata (1677-84), with an introduction by Mathers. It contains three key books of the Zohar: the Book of Concealed Mystery (Sifra di-Tzeniuta), the Greater Holy Assembly (Idra Rabba) and the Lesser Holy Assembly (Idra Zuta). These describe in daring anthropomorphic imagery the emanation of the divine 'countenances': the Ancient of Days or Vast Countenance (Arikh Anpin) and the Lesser Countenance (Zeir Anpin), their heads, beards and features, and the balancing of mercy and severity in the structure of the sefirot. Mathers, a founder of the Golden Dawn, introduced the Kabbalah to the English occult revival through this work, which became a foundational text for Hermetic Qabalah.

title: Sha'ar HaGilgulim (The Gate of Reincarnations)
author: Chaim Vital (Sefaria Community trans)
description: Sha'ar HaGilgulim (The Gate of Reincarnations) by Rabbi Chaim Vital, recording the teachings of his master Isaac Luria, here in the community English translation from Sefaria. Part of the Shemonah She'arim (Eight Gates), it is the classic Kabbalistic treatise on reincarnation (gilgul) and the structure of the soul. It explains the five levels of the soul (nefesh, ruach, neshamah, chayah and yechidah), the roots of souls in the primordial Adam, the sparks scattered through the Fall and their rectification across lifetimes, soul impregnation (ibbur) and spirit possession, how the soul-roots of biblical figures such as Cain, Abel, Moses and the patriarchs reappear in later sages, and the reasons for suffering and particular commandments in terms of tikkun. It also contains Vital's account of Luria's own soul and his circle. It is the fundamental source for Jewish teaching on reincarnation.

title: The Legends of the Jews, Vol. 1
author: Louis Ginzberg
description: The Legends of the Jews, Volume 1, by Louis Ginzberg (Philadelphia: Jewish Publication Society, 1909), translated from the German manuscript by Henrietta Szold. Ginzberg, the great Talmudic scholar of the Jewish Theological Seminary, wove thousands of passages from the Talmud, Midrash, apocrypha, pseudepigrapha, Kabbalistic works and medieval folklore into a continuous retelling of biblical history. This first volume runs from the creation of the world through the patriarchs to Jacob: the pre-existent Torah, the creation of the heavens, earth and angels, Adam and Lilith, the fall, Cain and Abel, Enoch, the fallen angels and the giants, Noah and the flood, the tower of Babel, and the lives of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Its later volumes include extensive source notes. It remains the most comprehensive anthology of Jewish legend and an indispensable reference for aggadah and mythic themes.

title: The Palm Tree of Deborah (Tomer Devorah)
author: Moses Cordovero (Nataf trans)
description: Tomer Devorah (The Palm Tree of Deborah) by Rabbi Moses Cordovero (the Ramak, 1522-1570), here in an English translation (the index credits Nataf). A short classic of Kabbalistic ethics written in Safed, it opens with the principle that a person should resemble the Creator, being configured 'in the secret of the Highest Form' in both image and likeness. The first chapter expounds the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy from Micah 7:18-20 as patterns for human conduct: patience, forgiveness, bearing insult, and loving even those who wrong us. Following chapters show how to imitate each of the ten sefirot, from the humility of Keter and the wisdom of Chokhmah through the kindness of Chesed, the restraint of Gevurah and the beauty of Tiferet, to the receptive Malkhut, in daily behaviour, thought and speech. It is one of the most influential works of Jewish musar and mystical ethics, translating sefirotic theory into practice.

title: The Life Divine
author: Sri Aurobindo
description: The Life Divine by Sri Aurobindo (1872-1950), the Indian revolutionary turned yogi, philosopher and founder of Integral Yoga, here in the Sri Aurobindo Ashram edition of the Complete Works (2005). First serialised in the journal Arya between 1914 and 1919 and revised into its final form in 1939-40, it is his principal metaphysical work. Book One sets out the omnipresent Reality as Sachchidananda (existence, consciousness, bliss) and the descent of Spirit into Matter through Supermind, Overmind and Mind, criticising both materialism and world-denying ascetic monism. Book Two describes the ignorance, knowledge and the evolution of consciousness, the triple transformation (psychic, spiritual and supramental), and the emergence of a 'gnostic being' and a divine life on earth, culminating in the chapters on the gnostic being and the divine life. A major synthesis of Vedanta and evolutionary thought, it ranks among the most important spiritual philosophies of the twentieth century.

title: The Ten Hymns of Synesius
author: Synesius of Cyrene (Stevenson trans)
description: The Ten Hymns of Synesius, Bishop of Cyrene, A.D. 410, in English verse by Alan Stevenson, LL.B., F.R.S.E., the Scottish lighthouse engineer to the Board of Northern Lighthouses and uncle of Robert Louis Stevenson (privately printed, 1865), with some occasional pieces. Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373-414), a student of the Neoplatonist philosopher Hypatia in Alexandria, became a Christian bishop while retaining his Platonic convictions. His hymns, written in Doric Greek lyric metres, fuse Neoplatonic metaphysics with Christian devotion: the One as Monad beyond all, the Trinity as Father, Son and Spirit understood through Platonic triads, the descent of the soul into matter and its ascent back to the divine, and prayers for liberation from the body's bonds. Stevenson's verse translation, with notes, is a rare Victorian rendering of these key texts of Christian Platonism.

title: Commentaries of Proclus on the Timaeus, Vol. 1
author: Proclus (Taylor trans)
description: Commentaries of Proclus on the Timaeus of Plato, Volume 1, translated from the Greek by Thomas Taylor (London, 1820), in five books (the full work spans two volumes). Proclus's commentary on the Timaeus, the most important surviving ancient commentary on a Platonic dialogue, interprets Plato's cosmology in the light of the whole Neoplatonic theology. This volume covers the opening of the dialogue: the recapitulation of the Republic, the Atlantis story told by Critias and its allegorical meaning, and the beginning of Timaeus's discourse on the Demiurge, the paradigm, the generation of the cosmos and its being, drawing extensively on earlier commentators such as Porphyry and Iamblichus and on Orphic and Chaldean theology. Taylor's notes, typical of his advocacy for Platonism, supplement the text. It is indispensable for the history of Platonic cosmology and esoteric interpretation of the Timaeus.

title: Commentaries of Proclus on the Timaeus, Vol. 2
author: Proclus (Taylor trans)
description: Commentaries of Proclus on the Timaeus of Plato, Volume 2, translated by Thomas Taylor (London, 1820), completing his English version of Proclus's monumental commentary. This volume continues the exposition of Timaeus's cosmology: the creation of the World Soul and its harmonic composition from the mixture of Same, Other and Being, the circles of the Same and Other and the planetary motions, time as the moving image of eternity, the creation of the stars and the celestial gods, the speech of the Demiurge to the young gods, and the formation of human souls and their vehicles. Proclus interweaves mathematics, harmonics, astronomy and theology, with appeal to Orphic, Chaldean and Pythagorean authorities. With Volume 1, it is a key source for late Neoplatonic cosmology and for the esoteric reading of the Timaeus that shaped Renaissance and modern thought.

title: Theologumena Arithmeticae (Greek)
author: Iamblichus (de Falco ed)
description: Theologoumena Arithmeticae (The Theology of Arithmetic), attributed to Iamblichus, in the Greek critical edition by Vittorio de Falco (Leipzig: Teubner, 1922). This anonymous late-antique compilation, probably drawing heavily on Iamblichus and on lost works by Nicomachus of Gerasa and Anatolius, is the chief surviving text of Pythagorean number mysticism. It treats each of the numbers one to ten, the Monad, Dyad, Triad, Tetrad, Pentad, Hexad, Heptad, Ogdoad, Ennead and Decad, describing their mathematical properties together with the gods, virtues, elements, cosmic principles and symbolic names associated with each (for instance the Tetrad as the source of the tetraktys and the Decad as 'universe'). De Falco's edition, with Latin preface and apparatus, is the standard text. It underlies later Neoplatonic, Renaissance and modern esoteric numerology.

title: De Umbris Idearum (Latin)
author: Giordano Bruno
description: De Umbris Idearum (On the Shadows of Ideas) by Giordano Bruno (1548-1600), the Dominican philosopher burned for heresy in Rome, in the Latin new edition edited by Salvatore Tugini (Berlin: E. S. Mittler, 1868). First published in Paris in 1582 and dedicated to King Henri III, it is Bruno's first major work on the art of memory. The first part presents a Neoplatonic and Hermetic metaphysics: all things are shadows of the divine ideas, and the human mind can ascend from shadows to the light. The second part sets out an extraordinarily elaborate mnemonic system based on rotating concentric wheels, inspired by Ramon Llull, combined with images of the decans, planets and mythological figures, intended to imprint the order of the cosmos on the imagination. Made famous by Frances Yates's studies, it is a key work of Renaissance Hermeticism and magical memory arts.

title: The Writings of Origen, Vol. 1 (De Principiis)
author: Origen (Crombie trans)
description: The Writings of Origen, Volume 1, in the Ante-Nicene Christian Library (Edinburgh: T. & T. Clark, 1869), translated by Frederick Crombie, chiefly containing De Principiis (On First Principles). Origen of Alexandria (c. 185-254), the most influential theologian of the early Church before Augustine, wrote De Principiis around 220-230 as the first systematic Christian theology. It survives mainly in Rufinus's Latin translation, with some Greek fragments. Its four books treat God, the Son and the Holy Spirit; rational beings, their pre-existence, fall and descent into bodies according to their merit; the world, free will and the powers; the restoration (apokatastasis) of all things; and the interpretation of scripture through its literal, moral and spiritual senses. Some of Origen's speculations were later condemned, but his allegorical exegesis and mystical ascent profoundly shaped Christian mysticism.

description: The Works of Philo Judaeus, the contemporary of Josephus, Volume 1, translated from the Greek by C. D. Yonge (London: Henry G. Bohn, 1854), in Bohn's Ecclesiastical Library. title: The Book of Enoch
author: R. H. Charles (trans)
description: The Book of Enoch (1 Enoch), translated from the Ethiopic by R. H. Charles (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1912 revised edition, also issued in a popular SPCK edition in 1917), with introduction and notes. Preserved complete only in Ge'ez and canonical in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, this Jewish apocalyptic compilation dates from the third century BCE to the first century CE. Its five parts are: the Book of the Watchers, telling of the fallen angels who mated with women and taught forbidden arts and Enoch's journeys through heaven and the underworld; the Similitudes or Parables, with the mysterious Son of Man; the Astronomical Book on the calendar and heavenly luminaries; the Dream Visions, including the Animal Apocalypse; and the Epistle of Enoch with the Apocalypse of Weeks. Quoted in the Epistle of Jude, it shaped early Christian angelology and eschatology. Charles's translation is the classic English version.

title: The Book of the Secrets of Enoch
author: Morfill and Charles (trans)
description: The Book of the Secrets of Enoch (2 Enoch, the Slavonic Enoch), translated from the Slavonic by W. R. Morfill and edited with introduction, notes and indices by R. H. Charles (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1896). Surviving only in Old Church Slavonic manuscripts but probably based on a Jewish or Jewish-Christian work of the first century CE, it recounts Enoch's ascent through seven (in some recensions ten) heavens, guided by two angels. He sees the prisons of the fallen angels, paradise and hell, the courses of the sun and moon, and finally the face of the Lord, before being transformed and instructed in the secrets of creation, including a cosmogony that describes creation from the invisible through the great aeon Adoil. Enoch returns to teach his sons, then is taken up, and the text closes with the story of Methuselah and the miraculous birth of Melchizedek. It is a key source on heavenly ascent and Enochic cosmology.

title: The Sibylline Oracles
author: Milton S. Terry (trans)
description: The Sibylline Oracles, translated from the Greek into English blank verse by Milton S. Terry (New York, 1890; revised edition 1899). The Sibylline Oracles are a collection of twelve books of Greek hexameter prophecies attributed to the pagan Sibyls but in fact composed by Jewish and Christian authors between roughly the second century BCE and the seventh century CE, adapting the prestige of the ancient prophetesses for religious propaganda. They narrate world history in successive ages, foretell the downfall of empires such as Rome, denounce idolatry and immorality, and proclaim the coming judgement, the messianic age and the end of the world, with the return of Nero as an antichrist figure. Widely cited by the Church Fathers, they influenced medieval apocalyptic imagery (the 'teste David cum Sibylla' of the Dies Irae). Terry provides introduction and notes.

description: The Writings of Clement of Alexandria, Volume 2, translated by William Wilson, in the Ante-Nicene Christian Library (Edinburgh: T. & T. Clark, 1869). title: The Niche for Lights
author: Al-Ghazali (Gairdner trans)
description: Al-Ghazzali's Mishkat al-Anwar (The Niche for Lights), translated with an introduction by W. H. T. Gairdner (Royal Asiatic Society, Asiatic Society Monographs, 1924). In this short and profound late work, al-Ghazali comments on the 'Light Verse' of the Qur'an (24:35), 'God is the Light of the heavens and the earth; the similitude of His light is as a niche wherein is a lamp...', and on the hadith of the seventy thousand veils of light and darkness. He argues that God alone is light in the true sense, that all other lights are borrowed from Him, and interprets the niche, glass, lamp, tree and oil as the levels of human perception: sense, imagination, reason, reflection and prophetic spirit. He classifies seekers according to the veils that separate them from God. Gairdner's introduction discusses the work's Neoplatonic character and its influence on later illuminationist and Sufi metaphysics.

description: Initiation, Human and Solar by Alice A. Bailey (New York: Lucifer Publishing Company, 1922), her first book, which she said was dictated telepathically by the Tibetan Master Djwhal Khul. It sets out the structure and functioning of the spiritual Hierarchy of Masters said to guide human and planetary evolution: Sanat Kumara the Lord of the World at Shamballa, the Buddhas of Activity, the three great departments under the Manu, the Bodhisattva (Christ) and the Mahachohan, and the Masters of Wisdom and their ashrams. It describes the path of discipleship and the five major initiations, the role of the Hierophant, the rod of initiation, the oath, the Word, the secrets revealed at each stage, and the solar and cosmic dimensions of initiation. Drawing on and reworking Theosophy, it was foundational for Bailey's Arcane School and much of the later New Age movement, including the idea of the 'Great Invocation'.

title: The Secret Doctrine, Vol. 1
author: H. P. Blavatsky
description: The Secret Doctrine: The Synthesis of Science, Religion and Philosophy, Volume 1 (Cosmogenesis), by H. P. Blavatsky (first published London, 1888), here in the edition divided into separate volumes. The founding scripture of modern Theosophy, it presents commentaries on the 'Stanzas of Dzyan', which Blavatsky claimed to derive from an ancient secret text. After the Proem setting out the three fundamental propositions (an omnipresent, eternal, boundless principle; the periodicity of universal cycles; and the fundamental identity of all souls with the Over-Soul and their obligatory pilgrimage through the cycle of incarnation), it describes the emergence of the cosmos from the dark, undifferentiated Absolute, the awakening of the universe, the differentiation of the elements and planes, the hierarchies of Dhyan Chohans, the planetary chains and rounds. It supports its claims with references to Hindu, Buddhist, Kabbalistic, Hermetic, Egyptian and Greek sources and critiques of contemporary science.

title: The Secret Doctrine, Vol. 2
author: H. P. Blavatsky
description: The Secret Doctrine, Volume 2, by H. P. Blavatsky, from the multi-volume edition of her 1888 magnum opus. This part continues the exposition of Cosmogenesis with its extensive commentary on symbolism: the 'Symbolism of the Archaic Teachings' explores the universal language of myth and the esoteric meaning of the primordial symbols, among them the egg, the lotus, the cross and circle, the serpent and dragon, the Deluge and the sacred numbers and geometry, together with the doctrine of the Logos and of the hierarchies of spiritual beings, as well as science versus occultism on matter, force and the ether. Blavatsky compares Hindu, Chaldean, Egyptian, Kabbalistic and Christian traditions to argue for a single primordial wisdom religion. Because volume divisions differ between editions, readers should check the table of contents for the exact sections included.

title: The Secret Doctrine, Vol. 3
author: H. P. Blavatsky
description: The Secret Doctrine, Volume 3, by H. P. Blavatsky, from the multi-volume edition of her 1888 work. This part is chiefly devoted to Anthropogenesis, the esoteric history of humanity based on further Stanzas of Dzyan. Blavatsky describes the evolution of humankind through seven 'root races': the ethereal, sexless first race of the Imperishable Sacred Land, the Hyperborean second race, the Lemurian third race, in which humanity separated into sexes and received mind from the Manasaputras or 'Sons of Mind', the giant Atlanteans of the fourth race and their catastrophic destruction, and the present fifth (Aryan) race. She interweaves myths of giants, fallen angels, the Flood and lost continents with critiques of Darwinian evolution. These racial theories reflect nineteenth-century thinking and are now widely criticised. Volume divisions vary between editions, so readers should consult the contents.

title: The Secret Doctrine, Vol. 4
author: H. P. Blavatsky
description: The Secret Doctrine, Volume 4, by H. P. Blavatsky, from the multi-volume edition of her 1888 work. This part continues and concludes Anthropogenesis, with Blavatsky's commentary on the symbolism of the archaic teachings concerning humanity: the sacred animals and the zodiac, the serpents and dragons as symbols of divine wisdom and of the Atlantean adepts, the war in heaven and the fall of the angels interpreted esoterically, the 'Holy of Holies' and the mysteries of sex and creation, the cross and the swastika, the Mysteries of the Hebdomad (the number seven in nature and religion), and addenda on science versus the occult doctrine of human origins. It closes the synthesis of science, religion and philosophy that Blavatsky offered as a revelation of the ancient wisdom religion behind all faiths. title: A New and Complete Illustration of the Celestial Science of Astrology
author: Ebenezer Sibly
description: A New and Complete Illustration of the Celestial Science of Astrology, or the Art of Foretelling Future Events and Contingencies by the Aspects, Positions and Influences of the Heavenly Bodies, by Ebenezer Sibly (1751-c. 1799), the English physician, astrologer and Freemason (first published in parts from 1784 and reissued many times). Its title page describes it as 'founded on natural philosophy, scripture, reason and the mathematics', demonstrating 'the abstruse doctrine of the stars, of magic, divination, exorcism and familiarity with spirits', the calculation of nativities and horary questions, drawn from the writings of over five hundred authors. Its four parts cover astrological principles and the planets, signs and houses, the calculation and judgement of nativities, horary astrology, and the occult sciences of magic, spirits and witchcraft. It contains the famous horoscope of the United States (the 'Sibly chart' for 4 July 1776) and many engraved plates. It was hugely influential in reviving English astrology.

title: Astrology As It Is, Not As It Has Been Represented
author: Zadkiel
description: Astrology As It Is, Not As It Has Been Represented: A Compendium, by an author writing under the pseudonym 'Zadkiel', the name used by several nineteenth-century English astrologers and almanac makers. The book defends astrology as a rational science of planetary influence, against what it presents as caricature and misrepresentation by its critics, and gives a compendium of its principles and their application. Topics include the nature and influences of the planets on the mind and body, the signs and houses, aspects, the calculation and judgement of nativities, and illustrative horoscopes of notable persons (for example the Rev. Edward Irving), together with discussion of rival astrologers such as Raphael. It reflects the Victorian revival of popular astrology. The precise identity of the author and the date of this edition are not confirmed here.

title: Heliocentric Astrology (1921 Edition)
author: Holmes W. Merton
description: Heliocentric Astrology, or Essentials of Astronomy and Solar Mentality, with Tables of Ephemeris, by Holmes W. Merton (writing as Yarmo Vedra), here in the 1921 edition (published by David McKay, Philadelphia). Merton advocates an astrology based on the heliocentric (Sun-centred) positions of the planets rather than the traditional geocentric chart, arguing that it reflects the true astronomical order and the solar source of life and mind. The book explains basic astronomy, the planets' heliocentric motions and their characteristics, the zodiac signs and their influence on character and talents ('solar mentality'), and how to set up and read a heliocentric chart using the included ephemeris tables. It is a pioneering work of the heliocentric astrology movement and a companion to the 1910 edition also in the library.

author: Magnus Jensen
description: Everybody's Astrology by Magnus Jensen, an early twentieth-century popular introduction to astrology, here from an Internet Archive scan. Written for the general reader, it explains in plain language the signs of the zodiac and the character traits, talents, health tendencies and compatibilities associated with being born under each, the influence of the planets, and simple methods for interpreting a birth chart. It belongs to the wave of accessible astrology handbooks published in Britain and America in the early twentieth century, when astrology spread to a mass audience through magazines and almanacs. The text, produced by optical character recognition, contains some errors.

title: The Sixteen Principal Stars
author: Joseph G. Dalton
description: The Sixteen Principal Stars, 1824-1948, by Joseph G. Dalton (1898), the American astronomer-astrologer and author of The Spherical Basis of Astrology. A technical work for practising astrologers, it gives tables of the positions (longitude, latitude and declination) of sixteen of the brightest and most astrologically significant fixed stars, such as Aldebaran, Regulus, Spica, Antares and Fomalhaut, calculated for the years 1824 to 1948 with allowance for precession, so that their influence can be included in nativities and directions. Dalton also explains how fixed stars have been used in traditional astrology and how to apply his tables. It reflects the late nineteenth-century effort to put astrology on a more accurate astronomical footing. The text is OCR from a public-domain scan and may contain errors.

title: In Somnium Scipionis (Latin, Teubner ed. 1868)
author: Macrobius
description: Commentarii in Somnium Scipionis (Commentary on the Dream of Scipio) by Macrobius Ambrosius Theodosius (early fifth century CE), here in the Latin text of the Teubner edition by Franz Eyssenhardt (Leipzig, 1868), which also contains his Saturnalia. Macrobius comments on the 'Dream of Scipio' that closes Cicero's Republic, in which Scipio Africanus the Elder shows his grandson the cosmos from the Milky Way. The commentary became a principal channel of Neoplatonic thought to the Latin Middle Ages. It discusses the classification of dreams, the immortality and descent of the soul through the planetary spheres, the virtues, number symbolism (the monad, the seven and the eight), the structure of the cosmos and the planetary order, the music of the spheres, the zones of the earth and the antipodes, and the Great Year. It influenced Boethius, Chaucer, Dante and medieval cosmology.

title: De Vita Libri Tres (Latin, 1549)
author: Marsilio Ficino
description: De Vita Libri Tres (Three Books on Life) by Marsilio Ficino (1433-1499), the Florentine priest, physician and translator of Plato, Plotinus and the Corpus Hermeticum, here in a Latin edition of 1549, 'freed from errors' and with additions. First published in 1489, it is a medical and magical guide addressed to scholars, whose melancholic temperament (associated with Saturn) endangers their health. Book I, On a Healthy Life, gives advice on diet, sleep, exercise and remedies for learned people. Book II, On a Long Life, covers prolonging life in old age. Book III, On Obtaining Life from the Heavens, a commentary on Plotinus, explains how to draw down beneficial celestial influences through the world spirit by means of music, images, talismans, plants, stones, scents and colours. It is the central text of Renaissance natural and astrological magic and influenced Agrippa, Bruno and Campanella.

This volume contains Die geistigen Grundlagen des Lebens (The Spiritual Foundations of Life), first part, preceded by a biographical foreword. Solovyov, the leading Russian religious philosopher of the nineteenth century and theorist of Sophia (Divine Wisdom) and 'Godmanhood', wrote this work in the early 1880s as a meditation on the foundations of Christian life: prayer, almsgiving and fasting as the means of uniting the human with the divine, the person of Christ, and the Church as the body of the God-man. The anthroposophical publisher reflects Rudolf Steiner's admiration for Solovyov. It is a German-language source for Russian sophiology.

title: The Teaching of Vimalakirti (Toh 176, Thurman trans.)
description: The Teaching of Vimalakirti (Vimalakirtinirdesa, Toh 176), translated from the Tibetan by Robert A. F. Thurman for 84000: Translating the Words of the Buddha, the non-profit project translating the Tibetan Buddhist canon (Kangyur), with the Tibetan text and English translation. Thurman, a leading scholar of Tibetan Buddhism, first published his translation of this sutra in 1976. One of the most celebrated Mahayana scriptures, it centres on Vimalakirti, a wealthy lay bodhisattva of Vaishali who feigns illness so that the Buddha's disciples and bodhisattvas will visit him. In a series of dramatic encounters he outwits the great disciples, displays miraculous powers, and leads a discussion on non-duality, culminating in his famous 'thunderous silence' as the supreme teaching on the entrance into non-duality. It affirms that enlightenment can be realised in lay life and influenced Chan and Zen Buddhism.

title: Liber Scivias (Latin, Heidelberg manuscript copy)
author: Hildegard of Bingen
description: Liber Scivias ('Know the Ways') by Hildegard of Bingen (1098-1179), the Benedictine abbess, visionary, composer and Doctor of the Church, here in a Latin digital copy from Heidelberg University Library. Written between 1141 and 1151 with the support of Bernard of Clairvaux and Pope Eugenius III, it records twenty-six visions in three books, each described and then interpreted by a heavenly voice. Book I treats creation, the fall, the cosmos (in the famous image of the universe as a cosmic egg) and the human soul; Book II treats Christ the Redeemer, the Trinity, the Church as Bride and Mother, the sacraments and the struggle against the devil; and Book III treats the building of salvation through the virtues and history up to the Last Judgement and the new heaven and earth, ending with a cycle of songs. Its striking symbolic imagery made it one of the most important works of medieval visionary mysticism.

title: Philokalia, Greek (Athens 1893)
author: Nikodimos & Makarios (eds)
description: The Philokalia (Philokalia ton Ieron Neptikon, 'Love of the Beautiful of the Holy Watchful Fathers'), compiled by St Nikodimos of the Holy Mountain and St Makarios of Corinth, here in the Greek edition published in Athens in 1893 (the original was printed in Venice in 1782). It is a vast anthology of texts written between the fourth and fifteenth centuries by spiritual masters of the Orthodox tradition, among them Evagrius Ponticus, John Cassian, Mark the Ascetic, Diadochos of Photiki, Maximus the Confessor, Hesychios, Philotheos of Sinai, Peter of Damascus, Symeon the New Theologian, Nikitas Stithatos, Gregory of Sinai and Gregory Palamas. Its theme is watchfulness (nepsis), the guarding of the heart, the struggle with passions and thoughts, and continual prayer, especially the Jesus Prayer, leading to stillness (hesychia), the vision of divine light and deification (theosis). Translated into Slavonic and Russian, it sparked a spiritual revival and remains the central text of hesychasm.

title: Forty Homilies (Greek, 1857)
author: Gregory Palamas
description: The Forty-One Homilies of Gregory Palamas (c. 1296-1359), Archbishop of Thessalonica and the great theologian of hesychasm, here in a Greek edition dated 1857. The homilies were preached to his congregation in Thessalonica on the feasts of the liturgical year and on themes of Christian life. They cover the great feasts of Christ and the Mother of God, the Transfiguration on Mount Tabor, where the uncreated divine light was revealed, Lent and repentance, fasting, prayer, almsgiving, the sacraments and the moral life, expressing in pastoral form Palamas's teaching on the distinction between God's essence and uncreated energies and on human deification. They are a key source for the Orthodox theology of light.

title: Sepher ha-Zohar, Le Livre de la Splendeur Vol. 3 (French, Pauly trans. 1908)
author: Jean de Pauly

title: Sha'arei Orah (Hebrew, Italian manuscript)
author: Joseph Gikatilla
description: Sha'arei Orah (Gates of Light) by Rabbi Joseph Gikatilla (1248-c. 1305), the Castilian Kabbalist and disciple of Abraham Abulafia, here in a Hebrew manuscript copy of Italian origin. Written in the late thirteenth century, it is one of the most important and clearest introductions to the theory of the ten sefirot. Its ten 'gates' each correspond to a sefirah, moving upward from Malkhut (Kingdom, the Shekhinah) to Keter (Crown), and explain the many biblical divine names and epithets associated with each, so that the reader can understand the scriptural text and prayer as a map of the divine structure. It became a standard primer of Kabbalah, was translated into Latin by Paulus Ricius in 1516 (Portae Lucis), influencing Christian Kabbalah, and is still widely studied. The scan of the manuscript is difficult to read by OCR.

title: Ginat Egoz (Hebrew, 1615 imprint)
author: Joseph Gikatilla
description: Ginat Egoz (The Garden of Nuts) by Joseph Gikatilla, here in a Hebrew printed edition (the index gives 1615; the first printing was Hanau, 1614-15). Written in 1274 when Gikatilla was in his twenties and under the influence of Abraham Abulafia, it belongs to his early, more philosophical and linguistic phase, before Sha'arei Orah. Its title alludes to the Song of Songs (6:11) and to the nut as a symbol of the hidden kernel of mystical wisdom within its shells. It has three parts: on the divine names and the mysteries of the Tetragrammaton; on the letters of the Hebrew alphabet and their combinations, gematria and permutations (techniques related to Abulafia's prophetic Kabbalah); and on the vowel points and their mystical significance. It provides a bridge between philosophical and Kabbalistic understandings of language as the instrument of creation.

author: Ikhwan al-Safa
description: Ikhwanu-s-Safa; or, Brothers of Purity, translated from the Hindustani by Professor John Dowson (London: W. H. Allen, 1869). The Brethren of Purity (Ikhwan al-Safa) were a secret association of scholars in tenth-century Basra who composed an encyclopedia of fifty-two epistles (Rasa'il) uniting Neoplatonic, Pythagorean, Hermetic and Islamic, especially Ismaili, thought. This volume translates the famous fable known as the Dispute between Animals and Man, from the Hindustani version Ikhwan us-Safa by Maulavi Ikram Ali. In it the animals bring a complaint before the King of the Jinn against humanity's claim to superiority and mastery over them, and representatives of every class of creature argue their case, with humans finally prevailing only through the existence of saints and the promise of the afterlife. It is a celebrated work of medieval Islamic literature and philosophical fable.

title: Hikmat al-Ishraq (Arabic-Persian, Delhi 1920 print)
author: Shihab al-Din Suhrawardi
description: Hikmat al-Ishraq (The Philosophy of Illumination) by Shihab al-Din Yahya Suhrawardi (1154-1191), here in an Arabic printing with Persian material (Delhi, 1920), probably with commentary. Suhrawardi, executed in Aleppo at the age of thirty-eight and known as Shaykh al-Ishraq, founded the Illuminationist school of Islamic philosophy. In this masterwork he criticises aspects of Aristotelian logic and metaphysics as taught by Avicenna and develops a metaphysics of light: all reality is a hierarchy of lights emanating from the Light of Lights, with knowledge as presence and self-illumination. He integrates Platonic Forms as angelic 'lords of the species', ancient Persian wisdom (the xvarnah or royal glory and Zoroastrian angelology) and Hermetic themes, and describes an intermediate 'world of images' (alam al-mithal). It profoundly shaped later Persian philosophy, including Mulla Sadra.

author: M. Sprengling
description: 'The Manichaean Scriptures' by Martin Sprengling, a short scholarly article published in The American Journal of Semitic Languages and Literatures (1920), now available as early journal content on JSTOR. Writing in the wake of the discoveries at Turfan in Chinese Turkestan, which had recovered Manichaean manuscripts in Middle Persian, Parthian, Sogdian, Old Turkish and Chinese, Sprengling discusses the canonical writings attributed to Mani, the third-century Persian prophet who founded Manichaeism, as described by ancient and medieval sources, and how the new finds of Manichaean hymns and texts were beginning to illuminate them. Manichaeism, a dualistic religion of light and darkness that spread from the Roman Empire to China, drew on Gnostic, Zoroastrian, Christian and Buddhist elements. It is a brief article rather than a book, included as a source on Manichaean literature.

Maximus's teaching on the logoi of creation, cosmic liturgy and deification shaped Byzantine mystical theology and the Philokalia.

description: Ta Heuriskomena Panta (Complete Surviving Works) of St Gregory Palamas, from Migne's Patrologia Graeca, volumes 150-151 (Paris, 1865), in Greek with Latin translation, including the Triads in Defence of the Holy Hesychasts. Gregory Palamas (c. 1296-1359), Athonite monk and Archbishop of Thessalonica, defended the hesychast monks against the Calabrian philosopher Barlaam, who mocked their psychosomatic method of prayer and their claim to see the divine light. The Triads argue that the light seen by the saints, and by the apostles on Mount Tabor, is the uncreated energy of God, distinct from God's unknowable essence, and that through it humans participate in deification. The volumes also contain the One Hundred and Fifty Chapters, homilies, letters and polemical treatises. The Palamite synthesis was affirmed by councils in Constantinople in 1341-51 and remains foundational for Orthodox theology and mysticism.
